content.title: Ex-Virginia Lt. Gov. Justin Fairfax faced sexual assault allegations before murder-suicide
content.text: WASHINGTON (7News) — For families facing childhood cancer, the fear is already overwhelming.For some, it’s compounded by a new and terrifying reality: being told the life-saving drugs their child needs may not be available.That’s what happened to Bryton Zastoupil.Bryton Zastoupil was only 12 years old when he was diagnosed with leukemia. Photo: Zastoupil FamilyWhat began as what seemed like a stomach bug quickly turned into something far more serious.RELATED | Mark Cuban promises affordable, safe drugs made in USA. What's standing in the way?They call us a little bit later, they say, ‘Go to Dallas Hospital immediately,’” Bryton recalled. “And sure enough, the doctor comes back, ‘You have leukemia.’His mother, Kristin, said the diagnosis was almost impossible to process.Bryton's mom, Kristin, says she knew Bryton's cancer journey would be difficult, but never thought it would include a shortage of cancer drugs. Photo: SBGIt was just a surreal moment. It doesn't feel real. You almost think it's just a nightmare. This is not true, this can't be happening, not my kid,” she said.Bryton’s treatment plan was intense — a carefully calibrated regimen that lasted three years and included up to nine injections a week.“Thankfully, there was numbing spray, which helped, but it did still hurt a lot. Yes. It's kind of hard to describe,” Bryton said.Bryan had three years of cancer treatment, which included the placement of a port to deliver life-saving drugs. Photo: Zastoupil FamilyBut amid that grueling fight, the family faced something they never expected: uncertainty over whether the drugs he needed would even be available.“We had no idea,” Kristin said. “We just assumed these are very sick kids. He's a very sick kid. We're going to have the drugs that we need.”“Every two weeks we were holding our breath that they were going to be able to get enough medication to treat him,” she added.Experts say those shortages are often tied to the United States’ heavy reliance on overseas drug manufacturing — a supply chain that can quickly unravel when a major plant is shut down.One example: methotrexate, a cornerstone drug in pediatric cancer treatment.In 2023, a manufacturing facility in India operated by Intas Pharmaceuticals was shut down after the Food and Drug Administration found serious safety violations, describing conditions as a “cascade of failure.” The shutdown disrupted a significant portion of the U.S. supply.This crisis - which often starts with incorrectly and sometimes dangerously made medications from overseas sources with very little oversight - is something we've been reporting for years.Federal officials have acknowledged that drug shortages have reached record levels in recent years, with the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists reporting more than 300 active shortages in 2023 — many involving sterile injectable drugs like those used in cancer treatment.Studies confirmed the 2023 shortage compromised care due to forced treatment delays and shuttered clinical trials, disruptions that experts warn can lead to patient deaths.That reality caught the attention of billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban, who has launched an effort to manufacture generic drugs in the United States.“I mean, I can't think of anything worse for somebody to do with their company than to make it so it's harder and more expensive for a child to get their cancer medication,” Cuban said. “So we manufacture them.”We spent time with Mark Cuban at his Cost Plus drug manufacturing facility in Dallas, Texas - where he is trying to disrupt a notoriously entrenched, expensive and unreliable drug system with options that he says "need to serve patients." Photo: SBGIn a Dallas parking lot, just across the street from Cuban’s company — Cost Plus Drugs — is trying a different approach: modular manufacturing units housed inside unassuming trailers.Dr Oshmyanski says these trailers can go anywhere they're needed to produce medicine. .Photo: SBGInside, highly specialized equipment can produce sterile injectable drugs — and pivot quickly depending on need.“It's the only one like it, to my knowledge, not just in the United States, but in the world,” said Dr. Alex Oshmyansky, CEO of Cost Plus Drugs and a practicing radiologist.“Everything here is sort of built from the ground up to be able to address drug shortages,” he said.The system is designed for speed. Oshmyansky said they expect to be able to switch from producing one drug to another in about four hours.Dr Oshmyanski says within about 4 hours, the flexible manufacturing systems in the trailers can pivot from making one drug to a different drug. Photo: SBGThat kind of flexibility could prove critical in a system where shortages can emerge suddenly — and where delays can cost lives.Today, after three years of treatment, Bryton is cancer-free.Bryton Zastoupil got to ring the bell, signaling he was finished with his cancer treatment. Photo: Zastoupil FamilyHe says knowing more drugs could be made in the United States gives him confidence.“Having it made directly in America, we know it'll pass the standards because they have to make it to those standards,” he said. “And so that's what makes me feel better about having this whole market in America so that way we can make sure everyone can get it how they need it.”For families like Bryton’s, the hope is simple: that the drugs they need will be there when they need them.But significant hurdles remain for American manufacturers — including steep regulatory costs and a system that often prioritizes price over quality — leaving the broader challenge of securing the nation’s drug supply far from solved.Watch our documentary, including what our crews discovered outside Indian drug making facilities, here.Even though Bryton is cancer-free, he and his mom Kristin say they will continue to fight to make sure other families have a safe and plentiful supply of the cancer drugs families like theirs had to rely on. Photo: Zastoupil Family
